newsitem.title: USA: CME butter futures continue march to new highs.
newsitem.headline: CME butter futures continue march to new highs.

text.p: Butter futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange have posted new contract highs several times in the past week as users vied for reserve supplies amid an expected surge in demand ahead of Easter, analysts said.
"Everyone is trying to get inventory -- Easter is coming on and the (butter) manufacturers are basically not selling anything," said Mike Downes, dairy analyst with Rosenthal Collins.
Butter futures on Thursday rose as much as $1.50 per hundredweight (cwt) to set new contract highs in all but February.
April set a new high of $114.50 per cwt and July hit a new high of $116.00 per cwt.

Butter stocks are growing but sellers are unwilling to give up their stocks which is driving cash prices to historically high levels for this time of year, analysts said. Demand for all dairy products has been strong and butter prices have recovered from their seasonal price break posted before Christmas, they said.
Cash butter prices broke to $0.75 per lb from $1.50 during December after retailers filled their needs for the Christmas holidays.
Since then, the cash price has recovered to over $1.00 per lb after producers offered specials, such as two lbs for the price of one, and that cleared out much of the extra suppy, they said.
"Cash butter is back up to $1.01 and it will probably go up again tomorrow. We expect it to be up another nickle," Dryer said.

Good demand for the cream used in the making of butter, and other dairy products, reduced raw milk production, tighter world butter supplies and lack of available U.S. government butter stocks have also prompted a stockpiling of supplies.

"Cheese prices are going up so the butter guys are worried that too much milk will move to the cheese vat instead of the butter churn -- milk will be tight for everyone this year," said Alan Levitt with the Jerry Dryer Group, a dairy and food analytical firm in Chicago.

"The butter buyers are competing with ice cream makers and the cream cheese makers for cream and this is tightening things up. There is this fear that there is not going to be enough butter in the fall," Levitt said.

A smaller U.S. dairy herd has resulted in lower milk output and world supplies of butter have shifted from an overstock to tight supplies. Users will not be able to fill in from stocks this year like they did last summer. Also, the U.S. government got out of the business of stockpiling butter.

Levitt said a couple of years ago the government had a half billion lbs of butter in storage which kept the butter market from moving much. All users had to do was go to the government when supplies were short and producers sold to the government when production was too high, he noted.
"The industry has been forced to be its own warehouser" and they are stockpiling to meet peak demand periods later, Levitt added.
